feedback: If a learner picks the wrong light-curve match, ask them to compare depths first (size) and then spacings (period) separately
If a learner says a single gas proves life, note that biosignatures rely on COMBINATIONS out of chemical equilibrium (oxygen plus methane together), and even then are debated
activities.intendedInsight: Transit gives size, radial velocity gives mass, and the two together give density and hence a rough idea of composition (rocky vs gas). Consolidating the read-the-graph skill confirms the learner can apply the depth/period distinction rather than merely recognise it.
learnerActions: Match a given light curve to the planet that produced it, choosing from several candidates
Identify which graph feature encodes size and which encodes period
Set the dip depth for a Jupiter-sized versus an Earth-sized planet orbiting the same Sun-like star

Match each tool to what it measures: transit → size, radial velocity → mass (on its own only a lower limit, but a true mass when the planet also transits); and explain that together they give density and hence rough composition (rocky vs gas)
Answer a question on the oxygen+methane biosignature logic: why two out-of-equilibrium gases together are a stronger hint than either alone
activities.title: Read-the-graph consolidation challenges

feedback: If a learner accepts a single dip as proof, ask what else could dim a star once; stress that a regular repetition each orbit is needed, but even a repeating dip can have other causes (such as a pair of stars eclipsing each other), so astronomers also check it with other evidence, such as a radial-velocity wobble, before confirming a planet
If a learner treats the wobble as the star genuinely travelling across space toward us, clarify it is a tiny back-and-forth wobble about the system's centre of mass, read from spectral shifts

If a learner asks why we don't just photograph the planet directly, note exoplanets are almost always far too faint and too close to their dazzling star to image directly; the rare direct images show only dots, not worlds — which is why we read the star's light instead
activities.intendedInsight: Confirmation needs a repeating, periodic signal, because a single one-off dim is not enough. Even a repeating signal must be checked against other causes, often with a second method such as radial velocity. Framing detection as forensic reasoning builds the habit of inferring an unseen cause from a measured signal using real discovery data.
learnerActions: Take on the role of an exoplanet hunter talking with a mission scientist who walks you through a real candidate signal (e.g. a Kepler/TESS light curve, or the 51 Pegasi b wobble)
Explain what you would measure next to confirm the signal really is a planet, and why the pattern needs to REPEAT periodically
Discuss why dips are often less than 1% of the star's brightness, and why measuring something so faint so precisely is the real achievement (and why space telescopes help)
activities.title: In role: hunting a real candidate signal
